summary: This RFC describes the RPL Option, an IPv6 hop-by-hop option for RPL routers to carry routing information in data packets. This helps quickly spot inconsistencies in the routing topology.

plainLanguage.summary: RPL routers add routing information to packets that travel through the network. Each router can use that information to check the route while forwarding the packet.

questions: how does rpl detect routing loops
subtitle: An IPv6 option that lets RPL routers carry routing information in packets as they forward them.

tldr.problem: RPL networks need to detect routing inconsistencies, but low-power and lossy links limit how much control traffic they can send.
tldr.mechanism: RPL routers place a small option in IPv6 packets and process it along the route. When tunneling is needed, the option goes in the outer IPv6 header so the original packet stays unchanged.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6553 is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 9008, RFC 9685 and RFC 9914. These updates should be read with the original specification.

sections.title: Checking Routing Through Data Packets
sections.content:
RPL is an IPv6 routing protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks. These networks must limit control traffic, yet routers still need to detect and repair routing problems.

RPL includes routing information in data packets so routers can check the path when data is flowing. This makes repair activity responsive to actual traffic. The RFC defines the RPL Option for routers in the same RPL Instance.
sections.plainLanguage: RPL routers check routing information in packets that are already moving through the network. This avoids sending extra checks when no data is being sent.

sections.title: Where the RPL Option Goes
sections.content:
The RPL Option is an IPv6 Hop-by-Hop option, placed in the header immediately after the IPv6 header. Every RPL router along a packet's path processes and updates it. If a packet lacks the option, a router must add one before forwarding it to another RPL router.

The RFC also specifies IPv6-in-IPv6 tunneling for cases where the router must attach the option without changing the original packet. The tunnel header carries the option, and related ICMP errors return to the router that created it.
sections.plainLanguage: RPL routers read and update the option as they forward a packet. When they use a tunnel, they put the option in an outer header and leave the original packet unchanged.

sections.title: Fields in the RPL Option
sections.content:
The option type is 0x63, and its alignment is 2n. An 8-bit length field gives the option's size in octets, excluding the type and length fields. The fixed data includes the one-bit Down, Rank-Error and Forwarding-Error flags, five zero bits, an 8-bit RPLInstanceID and a 16-bit SenderRank.

The fields' detailed meanings and processing rules are defined by RFC 6550. The option may also carry sub-TLVs, but this RFC defines none. A RPL device must skip unrecognized sub-TLVs and try to process any that follow. An IPv6 node that does not recognize this option must discard the packet.
sections.plainLanguage: The option carries three flags, an instance identifier and a sender rank. A router that does not recognize the option must discard the packet, while a RPL device skips sub-TLVs it does not recognize.

sections.title: Forwarding Between RPL Routers
sections.content:
Packets sent between RPL routers must include either a RPL Option or a RPL Source Route Header, and may include both. A packet with a source route header does not need the option because the source and intermediate routers ensure that the source route has no loops.

A router should put the option directly in the original packet when it is the source and knows the destination is in the same RPL Instance. Otherwise, it must use IPv6-in-IPv6 tunneling. A receiving tunnel endpoint processes the option before removing the outer header. If it forwards the original packet to another RPL router, it encapsulates the packet again.

Routers must keep the option within its RPL network. They drop packets for destinations outside the instance when the outer header contains an option they did not create. Tunneling adds header space, so the RFC recommends an MTU large enough to avoid fragmentation where possible.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers use the option only while a packet travels between routers in its RPL network. They remove a tunnel header at its endpoint and add a new one if the packet continues through another RPL router.

sections.title: Security Risks from False Routing Information
sections.content:
The RPL message security mechanisms in RFC 6550 do not protect the RPL Option. An attacker could change the Down flag or SenderRank to make routers believe a routing inconsistency exists. This can make them reset a Trickle timer and send DIO messages more often.

In Storing mode, a false Forwarding-Error flag could cause a router to discard downward routing state. Implementations may limit these effects to 20 events per hour, the recommended limit in the RFC. The downward-state attack does not apply in Non-Storing mode because only the Low-Power and Lossy Network Border Router keeps that state.
sections.plainLanguage: The option is not protected by the RPL message security described in RFC 6550. False flags can trigger extra control messages or remove routing state, so implementations may limit how often they act on these flags.

sections.title: Option and Sub-TLV Registries
sections.content:
IANA assigned option type 0x63 to the RPL Option in the Destination Options and Hop-by-Hop Options registry. The encoded action requires an IPv6 node to discard a packet if it does not recognize the option, and indicates that option data may change in transit.

IANA also created the RPL-option-TLV registry for sub-TLV types. The type field is 8 bits, and new values require IETF Review.
sections.plainLanguage: The option has a reserved IPv6 code, and IANA keeps a separate registry for its sub-TLV types. New sub-TLV values require IETF review.
